patient.chief_complaint: Two days of increasing confusion and difficulty communicating
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. V. is a 52-year-old man with NAFLD-related cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, MELD 14) who was brought to the emergency department by his wife for 2 days of worsening confusion, difficulty finding words, and increasing irritability. He had been increasingly forgetful over the prior month but the acute worsening began 48 hours ago. His wife noted he could not remember conversations from hours before, was not tracking time, and had been sleeping more than usual during the day while being restless at night — a reversal of his normal sleep pattern. He did not report dark stools, hematemesis, or abdominal pain. His wife reported that he had been constipated for approximately 5 days and had not been taking his spironolactone regularly due to dizziness when standing. He denied alcohol use and urine toxicology confirmed no recent use. Review of systems was positive for mild abdominal distension and decreased appetite over the prior week. He had no prior episodes of hepatic encephalopathy. He denied fever, neck stiffness, or photophobia. He had no focal weakness or sensory changes. His medications were reviewed and no new medications had been added.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade II), NAFLD-related cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, MELD 14) — precipitated by hypokalemia (K 3.2 from diuretics), constipation (5 days), and likely diuretic non-adherence; concurrent hyponatremia is contributory but not primary.

differential.key_features: Na 128 mEq/L — contributory but not severe enough alone (typically <120) to fully account for grade II HE; correct slowly while addressing HE.
Diagnostic paracentesis required to exclude (ascites present); follow-up PMN 82 ultimately rules out.
Thiamine borderline low; no ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus on exam, no MRI periaqueductal signal; give empiric IV thiamine before any dextrose regardless.
EEG shows generalized slowing with atypical triphasic-like waves but no electrographic seizures; benzodiazepine challenge negative on follow-up cEEG.
Platelets 88, INR 1.8 raise risk; CT head excludes hemorrhage.

optimal_actions.action: Send targeted laboratory studies: CBC, CMP, ammonia, magnesium, lactate, coagulation. Confirms liver dysfunction and screens for precipitants.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Confirms cirrhosis (low albumin 2.4, INR 1.8, bilirubin 3.8), identifies precipitants (hypokalemia K 3.2, hyponatremia Na 128), and rules out sepsis; ammonia 95 is supportive but not diagnostic.

optimal_actions.action: Non-contrast CT head — exclude structural alternate cause of AMS (hemorrhage, large stroke, mass) before any LP.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: No acute intracranial process; mild diffuse cortical atrophy — alternate structural cause of AMS excluded.

optimal_actions.action: Literature/guideline search to confirm West Haven grading, precipitant management, and lactulose/rifaximin dosing (AASLD/EASL HE management; West Haven grading; hypokalemia as HE precipitant).
optimal_actions.expected_finding: AASLD/EASL 2014 guidance retrieved; West Haven criteria and precipitant-driven management framework confirmed.

optimal_actions.action: Drug-interaction and medication-reconciliation review covering spironolactone, furosemide, omeprazole, metformin — confirm none are HE-precipitating sedatives; flag any CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, opioids, sedating antiemetics, antihistamines) and confirm lactulose/rifaximin dosing in liver disease.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Sedating/CNS-depressant medications identified; lactulose and rifaximin reviewed for hepatic dose adjustment.

optimal_actions.action: EEG — characterize encephalopathy pattern and exclude NCSE given atypical (non-classic) triphasic-like activity on initial study. Triphasic waves are classic but non-specific (metabolic encephalopathies broadly); main role is exclusion of non-convulsive status epilepticus where the differential supports it.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Generalized theta-delta slowing without classic triphasic waves; benzodiazepine challenge on follow-up cEEG excludes NCSE.

optimal_actions.action: Lumbar puncture for CSF analysis — only if meningitis suspected from focal signs or persistent fever — not initially indicated here. Must be performed AFTER neuroimaging confirms no mass effect.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: CSF results to confirm or refute CNS infection on the differential.

optimal_actions.action: Consult hepatology — coordinate definitive care, transplant candidacy assessment where applicable.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Hepatology / critical-care guidance integrated into management.

optimal_actions.action: Diagnostic paracentesis to exclude SBP given ascites and encephalopathy.
Draw two sets of blood cultures, aerobic and anaerobic, before the first antimicrobial dose
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Growth identifies the organism and its susceptibility; a negative or pending culture does not exclude the diagnosis, and yield falls once treatment has started

optimal_actions.action: Perform a diagnostic paracentesis and send ascitic fluid for cell count with differential, protein and culture, inoculating blood-culture bottles at the bedside
optimal_actions.expected_finding: A polymorphonuclear count at or above 250 cells/mm3 establishes spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, which is a precipitant that must be treated whether or not fever or leucocytosis is present

optimal_actions.action: Send urine for microscopy and culture as part of the infection screen
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Pyuria and bacteriuria identify a urinary source; a negative result removes it from the list of precipitants

useless_tools.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE workup.
Early-onset AD genetic panel has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the diagnosis under consideration.

sequence_constraints.reason: In altered mental status, exclude intracranial mass effect / hemorrhage on imaging before LP to avoid herniation risk.

critical_actions: Lactulose titrated orally to 2-4 soft stools/day (typical start 30-45 mL TID); first-line treatment.
Rifaximin 550 mg PO BID as adjunct (especially given recurrence risk).
IV potassium repletion to correct hypokalemia — hypokalemia drives renal ammoniagenesis and is a classic HE precipitant.
Empiric IV thiamine 100 mg before any dextrose-containing fluids — borderline thiamine 68 nmol/L warrants prophylaxis.
Diagnostic paracentesis to exclude SBP in any cirrhotic with ascites + AMS.
Slow sodium correction (≤8-10 mEq/L per 24 h) to avoid osmotic demyelination.
contraindicated_actions: Do not prescribe benzodiazepines for anxiety/agitation — they precipitate and prolong HE (use haloperidol or non-pharmacologic measures for agitation).
Do not prescribe sedating opioids — they worsen HE; consider acetaminophen at hepatic-safe dosing for pain.
Do not perform LP before neuroimaging excludes mass effect when the patient has altered mental status.
Do not correct hyponatremia faster than 8-10 mEq/L per 24 h — osmotic demyelination risk.
Do not anchor on ammonia 95 µmol/L being only moderately elevated; ammonia correlates poorly with HE grade.
key_reasoning_points: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grading + evidence of liver dysfunction + exclusion of other causes of AMS — ammonia level is supportive only and correlates poorly with grade (AASLD 2014).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleed, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia/hyponatremia), constipation, sedative/CNS-depressant use, dehydration, dietary protein load, renal failure.
Hypokalemia promotes renal ammoniagenesis by increasing glutamine extraction in the proximal tubule — an under-recognized but very common HE precipitant.
EEG triphasic waves are non-specific (any metabolic encephalopathy); their absence does not rule out HE, and atypical morphology should not deflect the diagnosis but warrants NCSE exclusion.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Diagnose hyponatremic encephalopathy as primary and pursue aggressive sodium correction.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Na 128 is contributory; HE remains primary given ammonia 95 with cirrhosis, hypokalemia, constipation, and characteristic exam (asterixis). Correct sodium slowly; treat HE.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Dismiss HE because EEG is not 'classic'.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Classic triphasic waves are not required for HE; atypical morphology is common in moderate HE. Pursue benzodiazepine challenge / continuous EEG to exclude NCSE rather than abandoning the HE diagnosis.
